utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin. Good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Ann Sutherland together with Denise Gustin, case manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham, I'm assisted by Vesna Anic. Mr. Ackerman, with the Court's permission, will be here after the first break. He is going to do the cross-examination of Mr. Sebire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So any preliminaries? Let's bring the witness in, please. We were in closed session. No? Madam Chuqing or in open session. Open session. Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you, sir. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, please, can you give the witness the text of the solemn declaration. Witness, could you please read that aloud once more, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Sutherland: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we left off on Friday discussing the arming of the Serbian population. I asked you a question in relation to that, and you replied: In 1991, that was the year when the Serbs started to arm themselves, in a systematic fashion, through the Yugoslav People's Army. And then you went on, and you said: They were armed also through other means and channels, and almost all of them in the areas of the right bank of the Una River, almost all of them had weapons. What were the other means and other channels that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means that they used private channels to bring in weapons from the Republic of Croatia, and then transferring it to local areas. So that they had large quantities of armaments in their possession. That is, into the territory of the Republika Srpska and SAO Krajina, armaments were being brought from -- for combat operations and they were bringing those weapons to the areas where they were, and they almost all had their armaments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the reserve police force activated at any time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But which one do you mean? Legal or not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, the legal police force.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September 1991, the republican Ministry of the Interior, that is, in Sarajevo, issued its instructions to mobilise the hundred per cent reserve force, so that after the incident, the reserve police force was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did the SDS do in response to this?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, last time -- sorry, I said that the reaction was that policemen from the police station in Bosanska Krupa, with vehicles and armaments, having been talked into it by Mr. Klickovic and presumably the Crisis Staff, went to the village Jasenica with their vehicles and armaments and stayed there seven days. After that they returned to Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any paramilitaries in the area?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the territory of Bosanska Krupa municipality, members of the so-called Suha Rebra, spare ribs, from Bosanski Novi, would often turn up. They were a group of criminals whom the SDS presumably manipulated and used for its own purposes. So that on one occasion, in Bosanska Krupa, a group of members of Suha Rebra group pointed a Zolja at the police station in the centre of the town, where a certain citizens's rebellion occurred, or rather, a protest, because of the way they behaved. So that they took the same vehicle and went back, or rather, left the territory of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. After the municipality of Bosanska Krupa was liberated, one could see many graffiti, saying "White Eagles," which means that paramilitary units of that group were in that -- had been in that area. They also had a group. I wouldn't know the exact name, but Dragan Prastalo, nicknamed Kudra, around Luska Palanka, who was charged with plundering the property of the Bosnian population in Bosanska Krupa, and that property was then taken away to the territory of Sanski Most municipality. And so these would be largely the three groups that were in the area that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa were these paramilitaries stationed?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not stationed anywhere. The first group was from Bosanski Novi. It's about 30 kilometres from Bosanska Krupa. So that they could come at any time and get to the area in no time at all. And when they would finish whatever job they were up to, they would go back. The White Eagles were in that area after Bosanska Krupa had fallen, because the graffiti had remained on the walls of the buildings in Bosanska Krupa. And the third group that I mentioned, that is, Dragan Prastalo, called Kudra, who was a tradesman from Luska Palanka, they were responsible -- charged with plundering Bosniak Muslims and they were in Luska Palanka, above the Bosanska Krupa municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any paramilitary units in Bosanska Krupa, stationed there?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any training grounds within Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We who were in the police had some information that we received from people who were in the area of Radici and purely Serb villages, Jasenica, and they had noticed there and observed that a largish group of men was being trained and that there were -- even had firing exercises with real ammunition. At some point there were some hunters who saw that and came to the police and made their report. But by the time we could check the information, such groups would disappear, because they were well informed, so that by the time we would get to the spot, they would be gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony on Friday, you mentioned that the Serbs wanted to establish a community of Serb municipalities of Krajina. It was from then that they put everything into this objective for the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. They were -- they established the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you aware of this occurring?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Martic incident, everybody realised that something was afoot, that something was afoot, because the war in Croatia was raging and the SDS frontmen, headed by Mr. Miroslav Vjestica and Gojko Klickovic, who was the president of the Crisis Staff, didn't even try to conceal the fact. They simply, in an un -- tried to partition the town in an unnatural way. That is, they were not concealing it. They had even prepared a study on the economic justification of such an idea, that is the partitioning of the city, and requested Mr. Meho Mahic, who was the president of the municipality at the time, to accept that idea at all costs. But I think it was simply nonsensical to partition such a town. I mean, it was impossible, it was indivisible and it would have meant partitioning it with some artificial line. So at that time we realised something was looming on the horizon and what was looming was the danger of war, and we realised something was about to happen and the only question was where and when in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sir, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please slow down a little bit because the interpreters are finding it difficult to catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd now like to show you a number of documents. Could the witness be shown P2052 [Realtime transcript read in error "P0252"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- time to change the transcript, but I think we are not now -- but for the record, we are not showing him Exhibit 0252, but P2052. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, prior to coming here, had you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have it on the ELMO, please? Not the B/C/S; the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think the document is double-sided, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you first see that document?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is a document dated the 25th of October, 1991, and it's a decision to establish a provisional assembly of Serbian people in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. So it was in November 1991 that you first heard about the provisional assembly?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown P2053.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a document dated the 25th of October, 1991. "At its session of 25 October 1991 the provisional assembly of the Serbian people of Bosanska Krupa reached the following decision, that the Serbian people living on the state territory of the Serbian people of Bosanska Krupa shall, as of 25 October 1991, cease paying all dues to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the present municipality of Bosanska Krupa." So when was the first -- had you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, yes, in November, sometime in November, I had the opportunity to see this document too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances? How did you come to see a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It just happened. There was a company, a party of people, and one of the present took out this document and showed it around. And he simply couldn't understand how was it possible to do something like this and how could such a decision request that dues to the legally elected municipality of Bosanska Krupa be discontinued and that all the responsibilities were being transferred to the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa and all the dues should be paid them, as of this 25th October 1991, saying that all these dues should be paid to the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P2054.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first see it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, it was in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that -- and this is a document dated the 25th of October, 1991, and it's a decision by the temporary assembly of the Serbian people to hold a plebiscite. Did you see the document before or after the plebiscite, to be held on the 10th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the referendum, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P2055.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, have you seen this document before; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, it was in November 1991 that I saw this decision for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is again a document dated the 25th of October, 1991, from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the provisional assembly of the Serbian people, a decision to hold a referendum to establish a municipality of the Serbian people of Bosanska Krupa, to be held on the 9th and 10th of November, 1991. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2056.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you seen this document before; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in November. I think it was towards the end of November. I also had the opportunity of seeing this document, the decision on proclaiming the territories on which Serbs lived and territories which belonged to the Serbs, state territories of the Serbian people. It was from the president of the temporary assembly, Mr. Milo Vojnovic, and it's been signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the document is dated the 25th of October, 1991. Thank you. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2065. I'm sorry, 2063.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that is a document dated the 27th of December, 1991, and it's an extract from the minutes of the third session of the executive committee of the Bosanska Krupa Municipal Assembly, held on the 24th of December, 1991. Could I take you, please, to the item marked "AD 3 A." Where it states: "The chairman briefed those present on the instruction on establishing SDS Crisis Staffs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and, in accordance with the said instruction, proposed the establishment of a Crisis Staff. This was followed by establishment of the Crisis Staff of the following make-up," and then lists 11 members. Sir, when did you first become aware of a Crisis Staff in Bosanska Krupa? You mentioned -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the beginning of 1992, I was aware of the fact that there was a Crisis Staff in Bosanska Krupa and that it was headed by Gojko Klickovic, the president of the SDS, who we knew was Mr. Miroslav Vjestica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2064, 2064.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated the 24th of December, 1991. The document is -- the signature block is Gojko Klickovic, commander of the Crisis Staff, and it's an order banning the use of firearms on the territory of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. And it states: "The public security's station branch station in Jasenica is hereby authorised to conduct checks, seize weapons, and take other measures prescribed by law." What was the ethnic composition of the police station in Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I should say that this doesn't refer to the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. Mr. Klickovic was the commander of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, and this order on prohibiting the use of firearms was issued for the territory of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. The legal public security station in Bosanska Krupa also had a branch in Jasenica, and the ethnic composition of that branch were almost 99.9 per cent -- almost 99 per cent were Serbs. Only 1 per cent of the men were Muslim in that police branch. So the Serbian authorities were actively working on establishing all illegal institutions, and with this order, the legal police station in Jasenica was turned into a public security station. An illegal [Realtime transcript read in error "And a legal"] public security station, a Serbian one, and they ordered it to act in the territory -- to act in the Serbian territory and allowed it to take weapons, to seize weapons. If there were Muslims, Bosniaks, in that territory, in such cases, they could seize weapons, or if there were others who happened to be passing through that territory. So checkpoints were set up, guard duty was assigned at these checkpoints. They would conduct checks. They would control individuals and vehicles, and if they found any weapons, they would confiscate them. This was an order which was issued to the illegal public security station in Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the transcript, page 10, line 20, it says a legal public security station, a Serbian one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your answer earlier, "An illegal public security station, a Serbian one," did you not?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned checkpoints. Whereabouts specifically were they established, and when were they established?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa was established by order of the SDS and its leaders, in the part where the Serbs were in the majority on public roads, on all roads, either from Bosanska Krupa to Sanski Most, there was a checkpoint at Vranjska, a place just above Bosanska Krupa, then the road from Bosanska Krupa to Bosanski Novi, the Serbian checkpoint was in Blatna. All the villages around Bosanska Krupa and guard duty was held by Serbs, especially at night. On several occasions I was present when the chief of the police, Mr. Semso Velic, mentioned at briefings that in the evening hours he had attempted to visit the entire municipality of Bosanska Krupa in a vehicle and that the Govedarnica checkpoint, at the Vranjska checkpoint, he was stopped by armed Serbs, who didn't allow him, as the legal chief of police, to move on into the Serbian territory of Bosanska Krupa. And they used weapons to threaten him and send him back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, I don't want you to take me as criticising you, but please try to answer the question and nothing but the question. I have the feeling that throughout this morning, you have been answering each question also beyond what is being asked from you. So please try to restrict yourself to answering the question, because otherwise you will take much of the precious time that we need for other witnesses too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2065.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated the 30th of December, 1991. It's a Crisis Staff order on the activation of the reserve police force, and it states: The reserve police force at the public security station section in Jasenica shall be activated in order to monitor transport routes to Radic, Vranjska, Arapusa, and the pig farm." First, have you ever seen this document before; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I've heard about this document. I heard about the fact that there was such a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this what you referred to earlier in your testimony when you said the activation of the reserve police, the illegal activation of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2073.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document entitled "To the great, wise, and respected Serbian people." It is headed "The municipalities of Bosanska Krupa." It then states: "Let us boycott Alija's referendum on an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina on 29 February and 1st March 1992." The document is signed. The signature block is the SDS municipal board Bosanska Krupa. Sir, have you ever seen that document before; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen this document. I saw it in the premises of the Bosanska Krupa police station on the desk of my commander, Lazar Stupar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we read the document, we can see down -- can you read -- I will read it for you: "The curse of Lazar will fall on each and every Serb who, despite everything he sees, knows, or hears, chooses to cast a vote at the referendum." And I quote: "He who is a Serb, a Serb by birth, and who casts his vote at Alija's referendum, may no offspring, male or female, fill his heart with joy, may his hands's toil leave his land barren, may he have no dark-red wine or white wheat, may misfortune plague all his kin forever." Sir, you said that you saw this on your commander, Lazar Stupar's desk. How did you come to see the document?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By chance. It was quite by chance, because the commander wasn't in his office. This document remained on his desk. The secretary and I simply saw the document. We were shocked by its contents. We were quite simply shocked by it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the secretary ever question Stupar about this document?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Lazar returned, comments were made with regard to this subject, that he was evasive and he avoided providing us with direct answers. He thought that at the plebiscite in November, they had voted for the creation of their own state, in which they wanted to live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is the Lazar referred to in that paragraph, the curse of Lazar? Who is that Lazar? Is he a historical figure? Who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He's a historical figure, the Tzar Lazar, a Serbian tzar. And here they're using him to say that if people vote in the referendum, that the curse of Lazar whether fall upon these people. So this is a Serbian historical figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2075.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that is a document dated the 10th of March, 1992, from the Executive Board of the assembly of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, addressed to the military post at Bosanski Petrovac. And it's a request for the arming of the TO. And it states: "In accordance with our needs, we are hereby enclosing a list of weapons for the Territorial Defence of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa." And then it lists a number of weapons. And then it says: "The aforementioned items are necessary in order to arm properly the TO of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa." Sir, those weapons wouldn't have been provided to the Territorial Defence, run by Hasim Djulic, would it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the Territorial Defence of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, and I think it was headed by Dusko Vojisavljevic. The Territorial Defence of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. There is a stamp here which shows that it's the assembly of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally could the witness be shown P2077. Could the witness also be provided with the municipality map P2020.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that is a document dated the 5th of April, 1992. It is a handwritten document. And the signature block is Crisis Staff commander, Gojko Klickovic. And it is an order to carry out a partial evacuation of the population from the following neighbourhoods and streets: Podvran, Hodzinac, Ljusina, Perna, and Zeljeznicka, Terzica and Titova. And excuse my pronunciation. Could you point on the map, please. If Exhibit P2020 could be placed on the ELMO. Could you point to the neighbourhoods that I've just mentioned. And what is your understanding of this order?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order issued on the 5th of April, in fact, orders the partial evacuation of the population from the areas that you mentioned. I'll point to Podvran on the ELMO. It's somewhere here. And the villages of Jlijici, Podvran had about ten Serbian households.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause there. For the record, you pointed to Podvran and that is just to the left bank of Badic [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Podvran is on the left bank of the River Una. I'm pointing to it now. It's somewhere around here. The Hodzinac settlement is -- also consists of about ten Serbian households, on the left bank of the River Una.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is just across --

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljusina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Drenova Glavic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. Ljusina, a Muslim, or rather, Bosniak village, and there were between five and ten Serbian households in Ljusina too. On the left bank of the River Una. The village of Perna, on the left bank of the River Una, the majority of the population in that village was Serb. The Zeljeznicka Street is also on the left bank of the Una River. It's almost right next to the Una River. And there were no more than five to ten Serbian households there as well. The Terzica Street and Titova Street were on the right bank of the Una River. It was in the central part of town, in the street near the mosque, and there weren't many Serbs there. You asked me what I thought about this order, how I understood this order. Well, my answer would be as follows: At the time the Crisis Staff was expecting fighting to break out, and it was in their interest to partially evacuate the Serbian population from the territory where there were Muslims and Bosniaks. To the right bank of the Una. And if war Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. broke out, to prevent these people from being surrounded by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document, both those documents. Sir, after this date, the 5th of April, 1992, were you ever on patrol in the area of Arapusa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-April, I think. I think it was the 18th or 19th of April when I and my colleague, Zdravko Megeljic, and Branko Saric, went to patrol the area of the villages at the foot of Grmec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just pause there. Do you recall speaking to a man called Stupar, but not the -- your superior officer, Lazar Stupar, but someone else by that name?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- briefly tell the Court the circumstances surrounding that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the checkpoint at the junction Hasani Svodna, we came up this illegal checkpoint with a member of the Serb police, whose last name was Lazar [as interpreted], and I remember him because that was also the name of my superior. I asked him to identify himself, and he showed me a certificate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript it says whose last name was Lazar and I remember it because it was also the name of my superior. Did you say Lazar or did you say Stupar?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stupar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He showed me a certificate with the -- with his full name, and it said that he had been issued with an automatic rifle number such-and-such, that he was a member of the Serb militia, and the document was signed by Gojko Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do with the document?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took this document with me, and when I returned to the police station, I showed the document to Chief Lazar Stupar and head of the -- on the chief of the police administration, Mr. Semso Velic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say when you showed him the document?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stupar always denied that there was any illegal police in Bosanska Krupa, but when I brought the certificate, saying that a policeman of the Serb militia had been made responsible for it and that there was Klickovic as president of the Crisis Staff's signature there, then of course he could no longer deny it and he admitted what all of us already knew, that there was in existence, there was in place this Serb militia, which was already active in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident at Arapusa on or about the 18th or 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Court about that incident.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Arapusa, which is a purely Muslim village, near or right next to the village of Osredak, where Serbs constitute a majority, and since the lawful reserve police force had already been mobilised, patrols had been assigned to patrol both the urban and rural areas. In Arapusa, at the -- a vehicle refused to stop when requested to do so by the legal police, and instead they fired a shot in the direction of the policemen and they returned the fire. So that two Serbs were wounded on that occasion, and then it turned out that they were members of the Serb militia. Two guys, I think their last name was Bokan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this incident ever investigated?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because there was still -- the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, still existed. Then investigating team was set up, with the investigating judge from Bihac. I believe his name was Slobodan Petkovic. Then Cetko Miso was the judge in the district court of Bosanska Krupa. A prosecutor, Munevera Ezic and that investigating team, went to the village of Arapusa and carried out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you part of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to Arapusa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many checkpoints did you pass on the way to Arapusa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first checkpoint was right below the hospital, at Govedarnica. That is what it was called. Set up by Serbs. The second checkpoint was at Petrovici. The third one was at Jovanka's monument. There was a large stone on the road, but they removed it to let us through to the village of Arapusa. So these were the checkpoints on the way to Arapusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived to Arapusa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating team was about to conduct the investigation on the site of the incident, but above Arapusa, on a hill called Nebesic, there was a significant group of people who were armed, and one could see a PAM aimed at a religious object, that is, the mosque, and there were mortars too there. The investigation was being carried out in Arapusa, and as it was under way, Mr. Mehmed Mahic and Gojko Klickovic came from Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's Mehmed Mahic, the head of the community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanska Krupa. He was the municipal mayor, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mahic, Gojko Klickovic, and yourself visit any other places in the area?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. In Arapusa itself, somebody had already said that between Hasani and Arapusa, JNA troops had turned up. And Gojko Klickovic said that the information had to be checked, so that I was at the wheel of the official police car and Gojko Klickovic was sitting next to me, and behind us, Mr. Mehmed Mahic, the municipal mayor. We went in the direction of that cemetery, and there were no troops there. However, Klickovic insisted that we turn back. But knowing that I had been visiting the area and coming across illegal checkpoints, I requested that we move into the depth of that Serb territory, some three or four kilometres. And then it really turned out that at the Hasani Svodna checkpoint -- junction we came across another checkpoint with a number of Serb civilians, that is, Serb people, 60 to 70 years old, about a dozen of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at this particular checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got off our official vehicle, Mehmed Mahic and Gojko Klickovic approached those farmers and talked to them. I was in civilian clothes, and I stayed behind with an old man who was not armed. And I asked him if everything was all right. I was simply trying to elicit some additional information. But he said. Yes, yes, yes, everything is fine. Weapons are here. We're all armed. So I said: But you don't have a rifle. Everybody else does. And he said: Yes, but I've got a pistol. And I asked him: Well, has SDS organised it all as it should have done? And Gojko Klickovic too, and he nodded to indicate that yes. And then I said: But what about the ammunition? I don't see any. And he showed below the road, about ten boxes of infantry ammunition, which was there, which means that everything was ready in case something happened. In the meantime, Mr. Mahic and Mr. Klickovic had completed their conversation with those men, and Mr. Mehmed Mahic came to me, and at that point I said: Meho, it seems that everything is ready here and the war is about to start.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the man that you spoke to tell you where the ammunition came from?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with Gojko Klickovic in the car travelling back to Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. On our way back towards Arapusa. And the conversation was more or less as follows: Is all that is going on necessary? Can't we find a peaceful solution? And the Mayor Mahic insisted on that and Mr. Gojko Klickovic, being the man that he was very arrogant, very bold, very sassy, if I may use that word, said very self-prepossessing, and he said at some point: Well, listen, Meho, if Muslims and Serbs cannot live together, then there will be a war and we'll live next to one another. And Mr. Mehmed Mahic nevertheless tried to dampen the things a little bit, saying that a peaceful solution should be found, that the crisis should be overcome by peaceful means. But to no avail. At some point, Gojko Klickovic said that a group of Serbs had been to see him and they had seen Muslims, Bosniaks, on the hill of Hum, clearing the trenches which had stayed over from the -- from World War II. And then he said: Well, if balijas are digging trenches on that side, then we the Serbs have you dig them on the other side. And that was generally the drift of the conversation. And meanwhile, we fetched up in the village of Arapusa once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date was Bosanska Krupa attacked?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st of April, at 1750.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period leading up to the attack, were there any negotiations being held?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The civilian authorities in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa have very actively engaged in devising a peaceful solution. Mr. Mehmed Mahic, as the head of the municipality, and members of the SDA, headed by Esad Velic, their president, Omar Kamenagic and Gojko Klickovic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and Miroslav Vjestica, SDS members. But throughout these negotiations, the Serb side kept insisting on the partitioning of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa, and that was something that normal people could not accept, could not go along. So that a political solution was not found and the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the final attempt to reach agreement? Where was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there should have been a meeting in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa, that is, in the municipal hall, and the meeting should have been attended by those that I mentioned. And I think that Mr. Fikret Abdic also came. And the chief of the Bihac barracks, General Ninkovic. So it could have been the 20th of April, a Monday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said the attack occurred on the 21st of April, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time of the attack, when the attack started?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was near the hospital. I was in the hospital compound. So it was 10 to 6.00 when the attack started, from all possible weapons that I heard for the first time on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see from which direction the attack was coming?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could see it, because all these fire was coming from the direction of Serb villages, Petrovici, Pucenik Vranjska. Those were Serb villages facing the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. The fire was quite intensive, quite fierce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the fire, were there any -- was the village being shelled? Was the town being shelled?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can -- Ms. Sutherland, you can go direct and refer him straight to the basic part, last page of his statement, and put direct questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how long did the shelling last?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling went on until dusk, and it was then when the light began to fade that the shelling stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did persons of Serb ethnicity do while the attack was going on?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: People of Serb ethnicity, 99 per cent of them had already left the urban part and moved over to Serb villages at the time of the attack. You could hardly find a single Serb townsman around at the time of the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did they do this?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Monday was the last day when almost all of them left. But that is what they did on weekends. They left the urban part of the town, just in anticipation of what might happen later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the shelling lasted until dusk. What happened the following day, the 22nd of April?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of April, at night, and early in the morning, an attempt was made to put together the defence of the town, made of the police, who remained loyal, and part of the population. In the morning, the attack -- the Serb attack started again, because they were out to take the town, and the fighting went on late into the night again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any infantry enter the town?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right. Later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of weapons did the Muslims have to defend the town?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatic rifles and PAPs. Some grenades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were these weapons from?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these weapons were in the police administration in Bosanska Krupa, and I've already told you that the town was defended by the police and the loyal part of the legal reserve police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you involved in any way in arming the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, in a way. I mean, to arm -- well, it was an active and reserve part of the police who were armed lawfully, those who were armed lawfully. They were all members of the lawful police, and they were issued with weapons, with automatic rifles or Paps, whatever was in the depot, because they were lawful members of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question may not have been clear enough. Besides the police, who were legally armed, were you involved in any way in arming the rest of the -- the remaining non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated a moment ago that the infantry came in on the 22nd of April. How long did the attack last in the town of Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, infantry entered a part of the town with an APC, so that was again in late afternoon, when they entered the police station, hoisted up their own flag, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, please pause there. Just answer the question. Was it one day, two days, three days, four days? That's the question. We don't want the whole story. I mean, I just want to know your answer to the question: How long did the siege of Bosanska Krupa last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the 25th of April. On the 25th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- everybody had crossed to the left bank of the Una.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you briefly describe for the Court the property that you saw destroyed during those four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me take over, Ms. Sutherland, because we are never going to finish like this. Was the mosque and the Catholic church, were they destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were houses destroyed? And if they were, who did these houses belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Purely Muslim, Bosniak localities, Ustikolina, Hum, all houses were burnt down there. Some of the Muslim houses in Mahala and Sokak localities were also torched by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution you stated: "All of the mosques on the right bank of the Una were destroyed by the Serb forces in the attack." Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution, you stated: "To give an example, all of the houses in the village where I lived, Ustikolina, Pazadjic, Hum were destroyed." Do you stand by this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also stated in your statement there were 300 to 350 houses. The houses were not even robbed. They were all just set on fire and systematically destroyed do you confirm?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also stated in your statement settlements like Sokak and Mahala which had mixed populations, only Muslims houses were set on fire and destroyed. Do you stand by this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A major part of Muslim houses. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any further questions, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have two areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did the majority of the Muslims move from the right to the left bank of the Una River?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time in early June that a number of Muslims were brought from the right side of the bank to the bridge?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 6th of June, 1992 when 702, I think, civilians from Sanski Most were brought for exchange to the bridge in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say exchange, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians who had stayed on the right bank of the Una, both from the area of Krupa and Sanski Most, were transferred to Bosanska Krupa, across the zeljezni bridge to the left bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were in effect transferred, not exchanged?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes, that is correct. Deported, deported from the right to the left side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last area that I want to ask you questions about: You do not know Radoslav Brdjanin personally, do you?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During 1992, did you ever see him on television?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the conflict broke out, so it was after the 25th of April, there was a meeting in Banja Luka, and Mr. Brdjanin was shown to have been present at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the context of the programme when you saw him on the television? You said he was at a meeting in Banja Luka. Was this a report of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was the news of Serb -- of the Serb radio television, so it was a news programme and they were either holding an assembly meeting or something, a convention, and Mr. Brdjanin was there and there was his signature as the president of the Crisis Staff of Banja Luka region or something [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on what day did you leave the town of Bosanska Krupa? You said, I think, the 25th of April.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We crossed to the left bank of the Una, Pistaline, Jezerske, that is where police units were and that is where we stationed -- were stationed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there for?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the liberation of Bosanska Krupa, in that area on the left bank of the Una, villages Pistaline and Jezerske and the urban part of the town of the left bank so until Bosanska Krupa was liberated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that occurred in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just going back to when you saw Mr. Brdjanin on the television: Did you know what position he held at the time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. But my friends who know him said that he was reading at the Banja Luka university and was an active politician in Republika Srpska, that is, in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you what position he held?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What position Mr. Brdjanin held?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A key position in the SDS and the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I have one more area, which will take me about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll have a break here and we will resume Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a couple of questions about the exhumation in Jama Lisac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2021, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how did you become aware of a mass grave at this location? Could you just point for Their Honours to Jama Lisac on the map.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But again, why should the map have already indicated on it the site which the witness is being asked to identify?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's like having a picture of a banana with the word "banana" spelled out and say: Can you tell me which picture shows a banana? So this document, as far as the question goes, particularly with the reference to this document, it will be struck off the evidence. The Chamber will not take cognizance of it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you a moment ago: How did you become aware that there was a mass grave at a location called Jama Lisac?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received information from a Serb who made a statement and we managed to obtain the information, according to which an area of Dubovik, which is where Jama Lisac is located, there was a grave in which Muslims, Bosniaks, had been placed. This grave is in an area that belongs to the Serbian village of Donji Dubovik. We informed members of the IPTF about this information and together with the international forces, they managed to locate that pit, that grave site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present during the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spent one day at Jama Lisac, and at the time they had already exhumed five to six bodies of Muslims, of Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. Yes, Mr. Cunningham. How long do you think you require? How much time for your cross-examination? That's to give us an indication on when to call Mr. Sebire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, my guess is that I will finish with him today, and I don't know the length of Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination of Mr. Sebire, but it would still be my earnest guess that we could finish both witnesses today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And Your Honour, with your permission, I think it might help speed this process along if I had the witness have his copy of his statement ready by his side in case it was needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's wise. Usher, please, can I ask you to give the witness a copy of his statement. Cross-examined by Mr. Cunningham:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Saran, I'm going to ask you some questions, and if at any time you need to refer to your statement, please do so. I want to remind you of what His Honour said about answering the question directly. I know you want to be home with your family as soon as possible, and I would like to accommodate you in that request. So to go ahead and get started, I want to talk to you about your background. You told us that your father was a police officer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that in 1991, you became a deputy police commander in Bosanska Krupa; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What qualified you to become a police commander? Did you have any special training in law enforcement?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a deputy commander at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. And I understand that, but that was your very first position in the police force. Did you have any special training at that time when you first became a police officer?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us in your statement and through your testimony that the municipality of Bosanska Krupa, the Bosniaks held the majority, of approximately 3:1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned today Mr. Mahic, who was the president of the Municipal Assembly, the mayor; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mahic, president of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanska Krupa. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please understand, with my pronunciations, I mean no disrespect to you. It's all new to me. There were also a number of Bosniaks in positions of authority when you took your position as deputy police commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, the president of the Executive Board and the head of the TO were all Bosniaks; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you must bear in mind the fact that before I arrived, the ratio was 4:1 in favour of the Serbs. The chief of the police station was Dragomir Kutlija. He was a Serb. The deputy -- the commander was Lazar Stupar, a Serb. The deputy commander was Slavko Ilic, also a Serb. The assistant to the commander was Branko Sarac, a Serb. And the assistant to the commander was Mirso Suljic, a Muslim, a Bosniak, and the ratio is 4:1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also told us that starting in about 1991, because of the recruitment of more Bosniaks, that it started to even out and be closer to 50 per cent Serb and 50 per cent Bosniak; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say it was 50/50. I said that a certain balance was established in the police forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say that there's a certain balance, what do you mean by that? I mean, what would the percentages be?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But there started to be more Bosniaks being recruited into the police force; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than Serbs or -- I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me find your testimony from last week. You said already in 1991, October/November, and I'm at transcript page 79 from last Friday, line 15 -- let me start from the top: "I am saying that the majority in February or March, that's when the balance -- there was much more of a balance, but already in 1991, October/November, what was then also present was the -- more of an increased employment of Muslims, Bosniaks. That's when this process of balancing began." Do you remember testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can tell me, fine; if you can't, that's fine too. Do you remember, roughly speaking, what the percentages were at this time frame in November/October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until my arrival, it was 70:30. Perhaps the balance was in favour of the Bosniaks by about 15 or 20 per cent. The balance was more in favour of the Bosniaks by 15 to 20 per cent. But I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did the increased number of Bosniaks mean that some Serbs within the police force had somehow lost their jobs?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us -- you told us about the chain of command within the police force, and the police chief -- and again I apologise for my pronunciation, was a gentleman by the name of Velic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was the police chief who was ultimately in charge of the force; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander-in-chief was Mr. Lazar Stupar, a Serb, that you've already talked about today; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is a statement, a sentence I take from your statement, where you tell us: Because of the chain of command, the head of police could not do anything without the commander knowing. Is that still your position today?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, the commander and the chief of the police station have to cooperate, and there are no issues that both should not be aware of. But there's always another matter. In that period of time, they may have concealed things from each other, if there was anything to conceal, and there were things that they wanted to conceal for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so that would mean, I take it, at times Mr. Velic would give you orders or information without informing Mr. Stupar.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the meetings, they were both present, the chief of police, the commander, the assistants, deputies. So this is the team that discussed the security situation in the town at the time, at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At any time when Mr. Stupar was still the commander-in-chief of the police department, did the police chief come to you, give you an order, without informing Mr. Stupar, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps he did. That concerned going to Arapusa, the visit to Arapusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to take you back to last week, when you testified about the change in the relationship between the Serbs and the Bosniaks. And you were asked when that changed, and you told the Tribunal -- your answer is at page 80 of the transcript from yesterday [sic], starting from line 12, you said: "Things changed. That could have happened already in 1991, when the Serbs wanted to establish a community of Serb municipalities of Krajina. It was from then that they put everything into this objective for the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. They were -- they established the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa. From then on, that's when animosity started to develop and increase between Bosniaks and the Serbs." Do you remember testifying that way?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that well before the formation of the Serbian Bosanska Krupa there were increasing tensions between the Serbs and the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the extent to which you assume that such tension existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I wasn't there, so I don't assume anything. But let me just talk to you about this. Do you know, do you have any recollection of whether there was a dispute over the erection of a monument for a Mr. Copic or in honour of a Mr. Copic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was not employed in the police. The writer Copic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, sir, I don't know. I guess my question is: Was there a dispute over the building of a monument for this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. individual? If you know.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that there was intolerance and I know that there was a certain amount of conflict, but that was on a political level, between the SDA and SDS parties. They discussed whether they should erect a monument to Branko Copic in the town, because such a monument already existed in the town of Bosanska Krupa. It was a political conflict between the SDA and SDS parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it Mr. Copic was a Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the monument was never built; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the location where they had intended to build it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But that was a source of contention between the SDA and the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One matter of contention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also contention over what the Serbian population perceived as the dismissal or lessening of Serbs working in municipal government?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any Serb animosity -- let me back up. During 1990 or 1991, did the secretariat for National Defence in the municipality, was that closed down?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know of living in that municipality, do you know of any discussion about a scandal involving some files that was a source of dispute between the SDS and the SDA?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us, briefly - and I do mean briefly - what was the nature of the scandal, and if it was one, and what was the dispute?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know all the details. I was not involved in this. But I know that it had to do with the files. Those who appear before this Trial Chamber will be able to answer that better than I. That's the chief -- the head of the municipality, who would be able to provide specific answers to these questions. All I know is that this happened and nothing else. I know that the files on conscripts had been taken away, and I know nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And is it fair to say while you don't know anything about the details, it was a source of a dispute between the SDS and the SDA?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no. I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And one area that was an area of dispute was the events surrounding the arrest of Milan Martic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that caused a great deal of animosity on both sides, both the Serb side and the Bosniak side; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I would put it that way, on both sides. There was more animosity, or rather, Serbs were angrier because Milan Martic was arrested, on the basis of an arrest warrant that came from Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go ahead and talk about the circumstances surrounding his arrest. And it's my recollection that you were not present when he was arrested but you were notified soon after. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you were notified -- what you were told, and I'm paraphrasing, was in effect that Mr. Martic had been stopped at a checkpoint in your municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a checkpoint where last week you did not know the ethnicity of the guards. Over the weekend, has anything come to you that would tell you what the ethnicity of the guards who were at the checkpoint was?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. In answer to your question, he said the police detachment in Bosanska Otoka was mixed. There were both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "But who was at the checkpoint at the time, I wouldn't know."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me just follow up on that last thing that the Prosecutor read to you. Over the weekend, do you have any additional information, has anything come to you that would tell you who was manning the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was more than ten years ago, and I do not know which policeman exactly arrested and brought Mr. Martic under custody to the official premises. The police unit in Bosanska Otoka was a mixed one. There were both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know from the information that you received that the citizens at the scene were very upset with Mr. Martic's presence in their municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were upset to the point, as you told us in your statement, that they wanted to lynch Mr. Martic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what you put in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how soon did you -- did you ever go up to the checkpoint yourself?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean where Mr. Martic was arrested?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was arrested at the zeljezni bridge, so he had gone through the checkpoint at Savor Celezni Most [phoen] in Bosanska Otoka a group of citizens identified him and he was stopped and then brought under custody to the police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you yourself, while he was in custody, while this incident was playing out, did you go up -- were you ever called up to the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for me to go to the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you agree with me that to many Serbs, Mr. Martic was considered a hero?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For those who identified with him, who wanted to create SAO Krajina and others, he was probably a hero. But to others, he was a criminal who was wanted, and therefore who should be arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what caused at least part of the incident was the fact that there was at least discussion about returning Mr. Martic -- turning Mr. Martic over because he was a wanted -- wanted for extradition I believe, out of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was wanted in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know from -- do you know whether or not that the Bosniak citizens remained around the police station after Mr. Martic was taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know whether or not -- let me back up. The citizens -- the Bosniak citizens had wanted to lynch him earlier. Do you know whether their attitude had changed at all?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to a point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that a large number of policemen were ready to defend Mr. Martic's safety, and that is how it was. That is, citizens couldn't get to Mr. Martic. That is, he was safe; he was secure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it is safe to say that someone in the police station felt that the threat to his life was a real threat and they were ready to protect him; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Velic, in his capacity as head of police, coordinated with the Bihac security services centre and the republican Ministry of the Interior, and it was crystal clear that Mr. Martic had to be protected, that had to be made safe in every respect, and the police did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand your answer, but as far as you know, the citizens, the Bosniak citizens, were still upset with his presence even in the gaol; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, ultimately, there are negotiations and Mr. Martic is allowed to leave; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was accomplished by means of the appearance of a federal official coming in from Sarajevo; correct, from the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The assistant republican minister, Avdo Hebiba.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at this time, the Ministry of Interior, that position was held on the federal level by a Bosniak; correct? If you know.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. But I think that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your position as a police officer, and you were a police officer after you returned to Bosanska Krupa, you were the commander?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I became a commander when -- since Commander Lazar Stupar stayed on the right bank of the Una, with the Serbs, after they crossed -- when I crossed to the left bank, there was no commander, so automatically I assumed this office, and in April 1994 I became head of the police administration, until November 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the seven years that you headed the police administration, from 1994 to 2001, did you ever discover in your municipality any documents, any evidence to show that somehow Mr. Brdjanin played any role in the release of Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me talk to you about another incident that happened in your municipality, and that's when the Serb members of the police force left the main police station and went to Jasenica to set up their station there. You know what I'm talking about, obviously. I think you told us that in your opinion, that they - and I may not have your words correctly, so bear with me - that they were talked into it by Klickovic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort -- you've described Klickovic as arrogant, bold, and sassy. Was he the sort of individual that could talk them into doing this on his own?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I remember, the stations, you had the station in Jasenica, and it lasted for about a week before there was intervention from the police union and someone on the republic level; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you got the point wrongly. The police unit at Jasenica was set up long before that. However, when Serbs left the police station and took away the vehicles and weaponry, then they went to the village of Jasenica and put up there, since they were almost 100 per cent ethnically pure, they put up at the police unit in Jasenica and that is where they carried their operations from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I stand corrected. I guess the point I'm trying to make is that this problem was resolved with the intervention of the police unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- do you mean the departure of Serbs to Jasenica and the problems that that produced?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the departure of the Serb police officers with their equipment and police cars to that village.
