utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the intervention of the republican Ministry of the Interior and the trade union who came to Bosanska Krupa, the problem was solved then, and Serb policemen returned to the police station in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know - and if you can confirm this, fine, if you can't, that's fine too - were the Serbs -- the Serbian police officers upset with the fact that in the Martic case, they saw the Bosniaks as siding against them, against the Serbs, and with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the dispute was about?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you have in mind exactly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I wasn't there, so you would have a better idea of knowing what made the Serbian police officers leave. If you know, fine, if you don't know, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose you should ask Mr. Klickovic that. I cannot answer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fair. But what you know is that when the Serbian police officers returned, the groups, the Bosniaks and the Serbs, were not working together in the police department; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't. The policemen continued their work. But it wasn't work in the proper sense of the word, because they were obstructing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were Bosniak police officers still patrolling with Serbian police officers?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Bosniak police officers still manning checkpoints with Serbian police officers?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most of the cases, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "In most of the cases, yes," that leads me to believe that there were some situations where only Bosniak police officers were manning a checkpoint. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot formulate it that way. It depended on the number of policemen. Where one could put together mixed patrols, Muslims and Serbs there, they worked together. However, there were instances where patrols were made only of Serbs or, on the other hand, of Bosniaks, Muslims only. It was very difficult to put together mixed patrols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it then that it would also be difficult to put together mixed checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I want to use that to talk to you about the incident at Arapusa. And you were not present when this incident happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the information you got came from other officers and other people that you talked to; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day I was on a different shift, and Mr. Velic, the chief of police, called me to the police administration and asked that I go with the investigating team to the village of Arapusa, to make possible an unfettered investigation on the site and I did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... talk to you about the investigation. What I want to do is right now find out which you knew about it when you were first assigned to do the investigation, okay? What you were told was that individuals had driven through a checkpoint; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since all of us, since all the policemen had Motorolas and they were always on, regardless of whether you were on or off duty, we could all follow things that were happening on the ground, so that I was aware of what had happened in the village of Arapusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to take it step by step. What had happened was there was a checkpoint that was manned by Bosniak officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a patrol, a police patrol, in the village of Arapusa, and the checkpoint was manned by the militiamen of the unlawful Serb police in the village called Topovak [phoen]. But they had to go through the territory of Arapusa to get to their village of Bokani. And at the request of the policemen, they did not stop their car, a Yugo, and a bullet was fired, and those others then returned the fire. And those guys were wounded on that occasion. I believe their last name is Bokani or Bokans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you told us that there were two individuals that were shot inside the civilian car; correct? Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a Yugo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this is something that you know from your investigation upset the Serbian population; right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so. I would say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you know from your investigation they were upset, they being the Serbs, were upset because they perceived this, right or wrong, as a police attack on a Serbian -- Serbian individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are -- they were lawful institutions which were doing their job, from the police to the judiciary, and I see no reason at all why the Serb civilians should be all that upset not to trust the judicial authorities, not to believe that they would do their job properly, that is, if there was any criminal responsibility, then that adequate measures would not be taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This calls for a yes or no answer. Based on your investigation, were the Serbs upset with the shooting? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say no. I think that the Muslim, Bosniak population was more upset, because Arapusa is a Bosniak village surrounded by fully Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me talk to you about the investigation that you conducted. And I believe you told us earlier that Mr. Velic, the chief of police, was the one who told you to go up there and join in the investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you did is that you joined part of an investigative team that went to the scene in the village; right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the investigating team was set up by the police station and we took two vehicles and went to the village of Arapusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to get there, you had to go through some checkpoints, including one, I believe, at Petrovici?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it was at this checkpoint that you said that you saw an anti-aircraft gun pointed at a mosque. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misunderstood it. That's not how it was. The first checkpoint was at the hospital, at Govedarnica, and there were Serbs there with weapons. The second one was at Petrovici, and we were stopped there, and M-53 was aimed at us, at our official vehicles, and that's a machine-gun. And the third checkpoint was at the very entrance into the village of Arapusa. The fourth one was up on the hill, on Nebesic hill, and that is where a PAM was aiming at a mosque. And I think two or three mortars, 60 to 80 millimetres each, and 10 to 15 to 20 men in civilian clothes and a few of them in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us that the gun was pointed directly at the mosque. Did you get into the -- get behind the gun and look through the sightings to see where it was aimed at?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't look through the sights, but I was 10 or 15 metres away from the PAM, which was aiming -- which was pointing at the mosque, at the minaret. I simply can't be wrong. I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from 10 to 15 feet -- excuse me. From 10 to 15 metres away, even though you can't get -- you were not in the seat looking through the sightings, that's still your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see it. You can see where a weapon is pointing and you can see that it was pointing at the centre of Arapusa, and of course the most conspicuous object there, and it was a religious object, a mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you tell us that, I'm quoting: "We were issued with everything that we needed to conduct the investigation and we went --" and I apologise to the interpreters for going so fast. Let me stop and start over: "We were issued with everything that we needed to conduct the investigation, and we went ahead about with it." That's what you said in your statement. I read that as seeing that you were able to do your investigation without any obstructions. Is that what happened? Were you able to do your investigation without any obstructions?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. As part of your -- among the things you did at the scene of the investigation is that you went with the mayor and Klickovic in a car, and I think one of the things you went to investigate was a report that there had been soldiers, the JNA, by the cemetery. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And again, we were -- we do not understand one another. Independent of Mr. Mahic and Klickovic, the judicial authorities and the police were carrying on the on-site investigation, and when that was over, in the meantime, the chief, or rather, the president of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Mahic, and Mr. Klickovic, arrived meanwhile. And afterwards, that conversation took place, how in the meantime, in the area of cemetery, in the direction of Hasani, some troops had turned up, and at that moment, Mr. Klickovic said: Let's go and check it out. And it was then that I, in the official vehicle, Mr. Klickovic took the seat next to me, and Mr. Mahic, who is the municipal mayor, took the rear seat, and we proceeded -- I mean, to the cemetery, which we just mentioned a moment ago. And some 200 metres from Arapusa is the village of Petrovici, and that is where the first checkpoint, manned by Serbs is, with a log across the road. So Mr. Klickovic gets out of the car, and talks to the civilians, who are armed, and the obstacle is removed and we go through. We reach the cemetery -- and up to the cemetery there were still -- there were -- that is true, no troops there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was -- you had a report from someone that there were troops by the cemetery. You went and investigated and there were no troops by the cemetery; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you did is you decided to drive a little further, and when you drove a little further, you came across some older men with weapons and ammunition that were there by the side of the road; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We came across another checkpoint, and I knew it was there because I had been visiting that area some ten days earlier. And there was a group of 15 to 20 armed Serbs in civilian clothes, with -- armed with PAPs. So our vehicle stopped. Mr. Mahic and Klickovic got off and went to talk to those people and I stayed behind with this gentleman who was not armed. And he showed to me about ten crates with ammunition left just below the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. Ultimately, you, Mr. Mahic, and Klickovic head back into town; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We turned back towards Arapusa, because that was the crossroads. The village of Hasani Svodna. And after that we went back to the village of Arapusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was on the drive back that Mr. Klickovic -- let me back up. On the drive back to the municipality, back to the town, there is discussion, and I'm not trying to get it word for word, but there is discussion, basically: Is there any way that we can reach a peaceful solution? And during the course of this conversation, Mr. Klickovic refers to I guess the mayor in a derogatory and insulting term; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wasn't insulting to the mayor, but his behaviour was. I mean, he was always an arrogant man. He always tried to exert authority and so on and so forth. They communicated normally, in inverted commas, because they saw each other, they met every day as a rule and they talked every day communicated every day. I mean, their political obligations made them do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say Mr. Klickovic always tried to exert authority. He always tried to be in control, to call all the shots, to be the boss. Right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was one of the big shots, maybe even number one, with respect to the formation of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the course of your examination earlier, the Prosecutor showed you a number of exhibits, starting with Exhibit 2052, and going up to page -- Exhibit 2073. And if you need to look at any of these documents, I'll be glad to get them. I'm not going to ask you about the contents of the documents. I just want you to see if you can recall that the documents that came from the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, all of those were signed by local party officials. And if you need to look at them, I'll be glad to show them to you. First of all, do you remember seeing signatures at the bottom? I'm just trying to save --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the transcript does not catch whether you say yes. Please answer yes or no. Because the interpreters have to hear what you say so that they can put it in the transcript. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I saw these images. I saw these images, that they were locals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And one of the signatures that you saw on more than one occasion was that of Klickovic's. I know I'm mispronouncing it, but you saw his name; correct, Klickovic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he signed that many times as commander of the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what he was doing was -- well, I won't ask that question. Let me move to the next area. I believe you told us that during this time, that tensions were rising, that you, as a police officer, had information about how the Serbian population was being armed. Do you remember telling -- talking about that last week and this week?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't the only one. In the police administration, we witnessed in a number of ways and heard a lot of information as to the manner in which the Serbs armed themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just focus in on one area, and that has to do with your discussion when you talked about how you would see JNA helicopters flying into Serbian villages. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that the war in Croatia had displaced many army families and that JNA officers many times didn't have a place to stay? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is: Were you aware of any JNA officers, particularly helicopter officers, who were living in Serbian villages in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any officers in the area of Herna [phoen] who were living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were there any officers in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You've talked about how the -- you received reports and investigative reports of the Serbian being armed. Let me ask you this: Was the Bosniak community becoming worried about this?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I realise that was a silly question, but were they, the Bosniak community, sufficiently worried about this that they went out and acquired weapons on their own to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is: Who could they have obtained weapons from? I don't think that they managed to obtain weapons. And I'm talking about the municipality of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So as far as you know, even if there were any attempts to acquire arms, the Bosniak population was unsuccessful in doing so, because there was no one to get the guns from?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about also how you discussed at least three different paramilitary groups that you became aware of, and one of them was either the spare ribs or the something ribs, and you described two other groups. And I think you said in the context of the paramilitaries, that they were presumably manipulated by the SDS for their own purposes. Do you remember talking about the manipulation by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, going back to number one, Mr. Klickovic, he would have the ability to do that by himself, would he not?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You talked about how the Serbians made a demand for everything on the right side of the river, and they wanted the Bosniaks to take the left side of the river; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was an -- although there were negotiations, there was certainly never any agreement reached upon the division of the municipality along the boundary line of the river; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was shortly after the negotiations ended that on April 21st of 1992, that the attack on Bosanska Krupa started; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the days leading up to the start of the attack, you had personally seen military forces in the hills above the town of Bosanska Krupa; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw armoured civilians and some troops, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you saw like a PAM, a PAM gun, and some other heavy guns and mortars in the hills surrounding the city; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you saw a large number of armed men and heard about an even larger number of armed men, armed Serbian men, in the area right around the town; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The attack starts on April 21st, and you leave four days later, on April 25th, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of April I was already on the left bank of the River Una at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I guess my point is this: The Bosniaks who were there, including yourself, put up a pretty good defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, correct me if I'm wrong: I think you told us in your statement that the police arranged for a defence that we could -- so that we could protect the citizens. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The only organised and armed formation was the police. The police attempted to defend the town, while the civilian population moved from one side of the River Una to the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many police officers are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire active force and the reserve force. That's about a hundred or 150 policemen. Not more than that. I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those hundred, 150 policemen had access to automatic weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all had legal weapons, because they were members of the police station. So they did have weapons which they possessed quite legally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that they possessed them illegally. I'm just trying to determine whether or not they had automatic weapons, and they did, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them. I said that in September, there was a depeche, a communique, according to which the reserve police force was to be increased by a hundred per cent. So all the policemen had automatic rifles or semi-automatic rifles. I don't know what the ratio was, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether if any Bosniak citizens, not affiliated with law enforcement, had any firearms and were joining in the defence?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. There were some people who would sell a cow or something like that in order to buy weapons from Serbs, and then they would make themselves available to the patriotic defence of the town. But it was a negligible amount of people, a negligible number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand what you are saying, but could you give us a number of these negligible people? How many do you think there were?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you remained in the area and you were present in 1995 when the town was -- the municipality or the town of Bosanska Krupa was retaken; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want you to bear with me on my pronunciations, but let me ask you this: Do you know whether the concrete bridge at Crno Jezero was still standing when you returned?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether the concrete bridge over the River Una was still standing upon your return?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was there, but it had been blown up, just like the wooden bridge that connected the two banks of the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when the concrete bridge and the wooden bridge were blown up? Were they blown up between April 21st and April 25th of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were they blown up?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have precise information. It was probably afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If Mr. Klickovic had given an order to blow up those bridges, would that be another example of him trying to exert authority he didn't have?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, in his documents, had an order -- among his documents, had an order to blow up those bridges in order to create a natural border so that Una would be a natural border and would separate Bosanska Krupa into two parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely why Mr. Cunningham is asking you the question, and it is precisely why I allow him to ask the question. Would Mr. Klickovic, in issuing those orders, would he have acted inside his powers or outside his powers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would have been within his authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we know from your testimony that those bridges were not blown up during April or May of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last area that I want to talk to you about, sir, is your testimony concerning Mr. Brdjanin, and I don't have the LiveNote in front of me, but my recollection is this: That it was your understanding, what you had understood was that Mr. Brdjanin went to university in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have understood my friends correctly, friends who recognised him. This is the first time I've seen him. So students from his generation who were with him at the Banja Luka university, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But my point is this: Those people that supposedly knew him told you that he went to school in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know, in fact, that he studied and got one degree in Sarajevo and another degree in Zagreb? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I've heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked to us or you testified earlier today that you saw him on TV in connection with some sort of political event. Do you remember, roughly speaking, when that was, what month, what year it was that you saw this?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the month, but it was in 1992. That's for sure. And I remember that it was a news programme, something like that, and Mr. Brdjanin attended that meeting and there was a scene indicating that this person was in question. There was nothing else about what was discussed at the assembly. I really don't know anything else. I don't remember the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I think you even told us that you saw his signature on TV, on a document.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that I saw a signature.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. Cunningham. The transcript did actually say that. We have got his answer so we can actually ignore that part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not document, but on the television, the name, the first and last name, appeared on the television. It wasn't on a document. You could see the first and last name of Mr. Brdjanin appear on the screen, as a participant in a meeting of some kind. I don't know which meeting. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand that you can't remember the exact date. I want to just try very briefly to see if you can try to narrow it down. Did you see Mr. Brdjanin on TV before or after the combat in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the combat in Bosanska Krupa, perhaps towards the end of 1992, but so much time has passed and it wasn't that important that it's difficult for me to remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, may I have a moment just to talk to Mr. Ackerman, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Just to clear this up, before I ask you whether you have a re-examination, Ms. Sutherland. Before the relevant part was -- about this signature business, you were reported here in the transcript as saying: Yes, it was news of the Serb radio television, and so it was a news programme and they were either holding an assembly meeting or something, a convention, and Mr. Brdjanin was there. And there was his signature as the president of the Crisis Staff of Banja Luka region or something. So what you meant saying was that there was his name on the screen, on the TV screen; no? Not his signature on some kind of document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Sutherland, do you have a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just two very small areas. Re-examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked in cross-examination, this is LiveNote page 53, about the three paramilitary groups, and that Mr. Klickovic would have had the ability to manipulate these paramilitaries, and you answered that probably. There was four paramilitary groups that you talked about in your testimony earlier today, was there not?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which the fourth one was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned paramilitary group from within the Bosanska Krupa municipality, I think in the village of Radici.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a unit, a working company that came from our territory. So we're talking about three groups that I mentioned, Suha Rebra, Bosanski Novi, Beli Orlovi, the White Eagles. You can still see their graffiti in Bosanska Krupa now. And the third group that was led by Dragan Prastalo, Kudra, from Luska Palanka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were the White Eagles from?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably from the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your opinion that Mr. Klickovic would have been able to manipulate these paramilitaries on his own?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about the attack on Bosanska Krupa, at page 55 of LiveNote. You said that there were between 100 and 150 policemen trying to defend the town with the legally -- with legal weapons. Approximately how many infantry did you see entering the town on the 22nd of April?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the infantry entered the town from a number of directions, but the main direction was from the crossroads from Vranjska towards the town and the hospital, or rather, towards the mosque in the centre of the town. So the attack was launched from several directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people did you see as part of the infantry?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the location I was at, it was not possible to see many people, but you could hear a lot of infantry fire, a lot of fire from infantry weapons, from all the directions that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall how many tanks you saw shelling the town of Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see a single tank shelling Bosanska Krupa, apart from a self-propelled rocket which entered the town and descended into Varos, the very centre of Bosanska Krupa, a self-propelled device.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified earlier today of hearing the shells coming from Serb positions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these were mortar shells, 60 and 80-millimetre mortar shells, recoilless guns, PAPs and PAMs, anti-aircraft guns and anti-aircraft machine-guns. Small arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I am curious about one thing. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You kept repeating on more than one occasion that Mr. Klickovic was in a position to manipulate practically all the paramilitary formations that you testified upon. What strengthens your conviction that this would be so? Why are you so convinced that he could manipulate paramilitaries coming from different parts of the territory, including the White Eagles that were, according to you, coming from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the simple reason that Mr. Klickovic was the president of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, and in documents that, in December 1991, in which he ordered that the Serbian police should arm, it is quite normal to expect that the authority that Mr. Klickovic had in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa could be used. And I do believe that he exercised this authority to ensure that paramilitary units carried out this work, instead of himself. So he was able to issue direct orders to those paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That brings us to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I just ask one follow-up question in relation to your question just asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not really, but I think we should leave it at that, Ms. Sutherland, now. Mr. Saran, this brings us to the end of your testimony, which means basically that, after having spent a week here and an additional day, you are now free to return to your home country. I wish to thank you, on behalf of myself, the Trial Chamber, as well as Judge Janu and Judge Taya, for having come over to give evidence, testimony, in this trial. You will now be escorted out of this courtroom by our usher and you will receive all the attention and assistance you require to enable you to return to your country. I'm sure that everyone in this courtroom will join me in wishing you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, do you think you will finish your cross-examination of Mr. Sebire?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. It's a little touch and go. I might. I might, I might not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you: When we come to the expert witness Patrick Treanor, how long you anticipate or how long you think you require your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution gave me his report last week, I think on Friday. I haven't even had a chance to look at it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you to read it and give me some kind of indication by tomorrow morning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that I can. I have other witnesses that I have to prepare. I'll try, but I can only put in a certain number of hours a day, Your Honour. It's probably quite long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ewan Brown, how long would you expect your cross-examination to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, on both of those, on this new witness schedule, the Prosecutor has given us, I have indicated that both of these witnesses will probably take longer than indicated on this document. Brown, I think, I would probably require a couple of days, just from looking at his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will resume at 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sebire, usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Sebire, or good afternoon. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Good afternoon to you. You will be cross-examined today by Mr. Ackerman, for the accused. And before you start with your cross-examination replies, may I ask you to repeat the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, may I have your permission to be seated while I question again today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to ask. Please feel free to do what is most comfortable for you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- at any given moment. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sebire. As the Judge told you, I'm John Ackerman. I represent Mr. Brdjanin. And I have a few questions to ask you. In the course of my questioning, I'm going to be referring to a number of documents, P2007 is your progress report of 13 August, 2008, that's year 2001 -- 2008 is the addendum of 16 May 2003. I want to refer to Exhibit S281 from the Stakic case, which is your additional report of 28 August, 2002. I'm going to be referring to your testimony from 30 May 2003. And if you could have in your possession all of those documents, it would probably help us get through this a bit more rapidly, which is what I would like to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, you can start, and the usher will make those documents available. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're employed by the OTP; yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sebire --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It takes a little longer for the interpretation to come through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a problem, let me know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long have you been so employed?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the 16th of September, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because you are employed by the OTP, your testimony in this case contains a certain bias in favour of the OTP's position, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to answer that question, since as an investigator, I was given certain investigatory responsibilities. I carried them out. The reports that I prepared are the results of the investigations that I made and the analysis of documents. I don't know if I can say that that is a prejudice. I don't really know what I can say about that. I can't give you any definite answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The word I used was "bias" not "prejudice," and they're similar, and I don't know how it was translated to you. Let me ask you this: You are here to put forward in the best way you can the Prosecutor's theory of this case, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of my work is very simply to make the connection between the various crimes that are mentioned in the indictment and the results of the exhumations and also to produce or to prepare -- to give a general vision of the exhumations in the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've presented that data that you have gathered together in the light most favourable to the Prosecutor, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presented them, that is, as being the results of the documentation that we had and the research that we carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you -- well, we'll get to it. I'll get there in just a minute. I want to just give you some examples of what I'm talking about. If you look at your first report that we have, which is that document P2007, your progress report of 13 August 2001, in your introduction you use this language, the first sentence: "This report summarises evidence obtained from forensic examination of individual and mass graves exhumed in the so-called Autonomous Region of Krajina." You chose to use the words "so-called" in front of Autonomous Region of Krajina. Doesn't that display some bias on your part against the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the -- that organisation and in favour of Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why do you use the phrase so-called." I mean, that was a real entity, the Autonomous Region of Krajina. It had a constitution, it had members, it had assemblies. It had everything. Why do you say "so-called"? To belittle it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Sebire, did you prepare your report in French or in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The very first one was drafted in French, and the following ones were prepared in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this one, this particular one, was it prepared in French or in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one we're referring to right now, from the 13th of August, 2001, was written in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have another question about choice of language that I want to ask you. In your testimony last week, May 30th, it's page 16690 of the transcript, line 22, you're talking about the exhumations from the site at Ribnik, and what you say in your testimony about the bodies that were found in those graves, these were -- and you use the word "victims" from the municipality of Kljuc. In what sense do you use the word "victims" in your reports and in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you're talking about the Ribnik site, the information that we received about the bodies that were exhumed from that site, they were prisoners who had been transferred from Kljuc to another destination. I admit that I don't quite remember right now exactly where they were transported to, but those people were never seen again from the time that they left Kljuc. When I use the word "victim," it is because we have information or reasons to believe that those individuals were killed, were murdered, after having been either in detention, -- we refer to them as victims that were found in the mass grave at Ribnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you refer to persons who were killed in the course of combat as victims, and have you so referred to them?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can speak about combat victims. You can use that word, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is that what you do? I mean, do you intend to use that word broadly to include combat victims, or are you restricting it to persons who you believe were murdered in violation of the law?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I made any distinction in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about in your mind? In your mind, how do you use that term you remember my question. Just tell me: In your mind, how do you use that term?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that there is absolutely no difference between someone who is a victim, who fell in a battle in which that person was a participant. In that case, would be a combatant, that is, a victim of that fight in which he was involved. Or the word "victim" in the more specific meaning of the word, that's an individual who was murdered, that person is also a victim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then would the Trial Chamber be safe in making the conclusion that when in your reports or in your testimony you use the word "victim," you are not suggesting that this person was killed as a result of the violation of some law but simply that the person was killed?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, for a very simple reason, because in my report it's made very clear that all the individuals -- I'm using the word persons in this case, all those persons who died during combats or for which the cause of death is -- no direct link with the events which took place, in the autonomous Krajina region from excluded from the report and this leaves the figures having to do with people who were murdered or who disappeared after having been detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we're going to come to all of that. So your answer, I believe, is that when you use the word "victim" you're talking about people who you have concluded were killed in violation of law?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you're saying it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about -- you basically have created two databases, and in your testimony -- it's page 1 -- 16685 and 6, you're talking about the second database, which has to do with proofs of death, and what you said on page 16686, line 1, that it was specifically created in order to have the information entered regarding declarations of the death, regarding the people who have died or were missing in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Can you tell us how many Serbs -- how many Serb names are in this database of the dead or missing from the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the figures in front of me, but as far as I can recall, there were zero, none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 16694, then, of your testimony, your being referred by Ms. Richterova to page 10 of annex 1, which would be annex 1 attached to P2008. That would be your addendum of 16 May 2003. And she is asking you to explain a discrepancy. And I don't understand the answer that you gave, and I'm hoping we can sort this out so it can make some sense. The question she asked was this: "In the second row, we have exhumation Hrustovo 9 Kasapnica, and we can see bodies 18 MNI zero." Can you just briefly describe the discrepancies in these columns." And now the transcript reads, the first sentence -- the first two sentences read like this: "Yes, I can. At this exhumation site, in fact, I should say it was a cream sign [as interpreted]," c-r-e-a-m sign, "that was visited by the Bosnian authorities." Do you have any idea what you actually said at that point?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I very clearly remember the question that I was asked about the exhumation site or the -- the crime scene, crime sign -- crime scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me read the rest of your answer. "On the basis of information from the sole survivor of a massacre, when the Bosnian authorities carried out the on-site investigation certain bodies were returned but not a sufficient number to determine the exact number of individuals present at the scene of the crime. Nevertheless, the report listed the totality of the victims. That is to say, the 18 victims that were involved in this particular incident. But the forensic report stated that it was impossible to determine the exact number of individuals present on the basis of the body parts that were discovered, and it is for this reason that one wasn't able to give a minimum number of individuals, and an arbitrary choice which we had to make was to say that this MNI number was zero." Now, if I understand what you're saying there, you're saying in the annex, we put the figure 18 bodies exhumed from Hrustovo 9 because we had information from one individual who told us that there were 18 people killed there, even though the body parts found at the scene could not support that number. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just about. If I could explain a little bit further about what I mean here on the subject. The report that we get about the work that was done on the crime scene in Kasapnica [phoen], in the report, the judge states that through the testimony that he received, he was able to establish there were 18 victims. And so as I indicated before, and as you yourself repeated today, the forensic pathologist said he was not able to determine the minimum number of individuals present at the site. And therefore, since -- we were not able to count the number of victims, we set aside the 18 victims that appear - you look in the line there - that were not considered within the zero being checked with -- in this list. If you look at the annex, having to do with this, which deals with the results of the works of the forensic pathologist, you won't find any information. And we do not have any scientific information to corroborate that specific incident, other than the fact that the human remains that were found there were found at a place that had been described by a witness and that -- and those were the victims -- the remains that he described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So basically, it's based upon a report that you received from a Bosnian judge from a Bosnian cantonal court, which was based upon information that that judge had apparently received from one person who claims to have been a witness and claims that there should be 18 bodies there, and that's how the number 18 gets in this report?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how the figure of 18 is in fact there. And that is also -- that's the number 18 which appears on the basis of the information from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Bosnian judge which is not taken into account in my report. As you just pointed out, there was no way to determine the number of victims and that's why we put in the number 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony at page 16699, you're talking about an exhumation that was done at Jama Lisac and the bodies of the two women, Edna Dautovic and Sadeta Medunjanin were discovered there. You recall that; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there was ever any determination made as to the cause of their death, either one of them?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cause of death was determined -- I can't tell you just like that from my memory. The forensic -- the forensic examinations were carried out by the team by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any of your reports, do you have information regarding the cause of their death?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For those -- in respect of those two specific victims?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you just give me a few minutes so that I can check in my report, my 2002 report, from August. In the August 2002 report, I did mention the identification of the two victims, and I give the cause of death of the victims who were exhumed on that site, without going into the specific details of each one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And said what?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the 51 victims exhumed on that site, the cause of death that we could say were wounds by gunshot, in two cases they were wounds subject to blunt instruments, and there were other ones, two other occasions where the cause of death was not established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two cases where cause of death was not established, do you know if that would have been Ms. Dautovic and Ms. Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've just said, I did not make a detailed list of the causes of death for each of the victims who appear in the report. And so I right now can't tell you whether or not those two women, what their cause of death was, and that remains undetermined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you certainly have no information about who caused their death, if it was foul play, do you?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to -- if you refer to the report that I prepared in 2002 for the Prijedor mission, in the information that's mentioned about those two specific victims, we have judgements declared that they were deceased, and in the judgement, information is given about the circumstances of their disappearance. For instance, for Edna Dautovic, there is a judgement that was rendered by the municipal Sanski Most court, which states that Edna Dautovic was detained in Omarska, where she was physically abused, and then she was put into a bus and supposedly for a prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question was: You don't have any information that would permit you to conclude who caused her death, and the answer to that is you don't for sure; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question of knowing who killed that person -- well, that's right. I cannot give you the name of that person. The only thing that my report states is that the last time that she was seen alive, she was in a bus that was leaving the Omarska camp. What is sure -- that's for sure. Anything else I can't add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same is true for Medunjanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have that report, the one you've been referring to. Would you just turn back to page 4 of that report, that report being your additional report of 28 August 2002 from Stakic, Exhibit S281E. You say in the introduction, next to the last paragraph: "The purpose of this report is not to make an assessment on the reliability of the documentation provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. Official bodies of Bosnia and Herzegovina, municipal courts, examining Judges, police officers and pathologists, produced the documentation, and this was done according to their own rules and procedures. It is important to stress the different objectives of the Bosnian authorities and the OTP forensic team. The aim of the Bosnian authorities in the exhumation process is principally of a social and humanitarian character, while the only purpose of the OTP forensic team is the collection of evidence. Given these different objectives and the variation in resources available to the two parties, it is understandable that the standards used by the organisations also differ." You're trying to tell us something there. I'm not sure we understand what it is. It sounds to me like you have some serious concern about the reliability of the documentation provided to the OTP by the officials of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Am I right in drawing that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what that means? Why do you bring it to the attention of the persons to whom this report was to be given that you cannot make an assessment on the reliability of this documentation? What does this paragraph mean?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simply, that most of the exhumations that we note in the various annexes that are in the report that I prepared refer to exhumations which took place between 1996 and 2000, regarding the forensic team from the OTP, we began to prepare the -- our reports after 1999, then we did some other ones. They were in Redak and Sinac [phoen]. We can, unfortunately, base ourselves for the prior ones only on documentation that was made available to us. All of the bodies were examined. They were buried again and we can simply say that we are relying on the documentation that was provided as such and that we were able to verify through testimony in respect of the cause of deaths of individuals who are identified, but it's true, we did not re-exhume the bodies and carry out forensic examinations on all those bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your answer, you talked about the ability to verify through testimony. Now, when you say "verify through testimony," you are not necessarily referring to sworn testimony in the courts of this Tribunal, but in many cases simply to the statements of witnesses who have not testified or have not provided their statements under oath. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But not in all cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll actually get to some of these cases in a moment or maybe tomorrow. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't think you'll finish today, Mr. Ackerman, I suppose we can even stop here. We'll have the meeting in my office straight away, because by 2.00, 2.15 maximum, I need to be home for some repairs to be done, which otherwise will take another two months to materialise. Mr. Sebire, you will need to come again tomorrow morning. I don't think your testimony will last long, but please make sure that you are here at 9.00 in the morning, or unless there is some kind of an agreement between Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Korner, at some later point in time. Maybe if it's more convenient for him to be -- to come over late in the day, late in the morning, rather than in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. I think 9.00 is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of June 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.38 p.m.,
